summary: This RFC specifies link and node routing metrics and constraints for Low-Power and Lossy Networks, for use by RPL. Unlike typical metrics based on hop counts or link costs, they reflect the constraints of LLNs.

plainLanguage.summary: Choosing a path for sensor messages is not only about distance. This lists the other things to weigh, like how reliable a link is or how much battery a node has.

subtitle: The menu of link and node measurements that RPL can use to pick good paths through battery-powered, unreliable networks.

tldr.problem: Low-Power and Lossy Networks (LLNs) have links that change quickly and nodes with limited energy, so hop counts and fixed link costs are not enough to choose good paths.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6551 defines a set of objects, carried in the RPL DAG Metric Container, that report node and link properties (energy, hop count, throughput, latency, link quality, ETX, link color), each usable as a metric to optimize or a constraint to satisfy.
tldr.outcome: RPL implementations can pick any subset of these optional objects. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted or updated.

facts.label: Object types
facts.value: 1 to 8 (NSA, Node Energy, Hop Count, Throughput, Latency, LQL, ETX, Link Color)

today: RFC 6551 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2012, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is the companion of the RPL specification in RFC 6550.

sections.title: Why LLNs Need New Metrics
sections.content:
Older routing protocols such as OSPF (RFC 2328) and IS-IS (RFC 1195) use quantitative, static link metrics. Low-Power and Lossy Networks (LLNs) behave differently. Their links, wireless but also Power Line Communication (PLC) links, change rapidly, and nodes have resources such as residual energy that change continuously.

This RFC defines the metrics and constraints used by the Routing Protocol for Low-Power and Lossy Networks (RPL, RFC 6550) to compute paths. A constraint acts as a filter that prunes links and nodes that do not qualify, for example only mains-powered nodes. A metric is a quantitative value used to evaluate path cost. The best path satisfies every constraint and has the lowest cost for the chosen metrics.

All the objects are OPTIONAL for an RPL implementation. One implementation may use a single metric and no constraint, while another may use many. The choice of Objective Function, which says how to build the DAG, is out of scope: the metrics are decoupled from it.
sections.plainLanguage: Normal networks mostly care about how short a route is. Tiny battery sensors also need to care about weak signals and low batteries, so this RFC gives them more things to measure.

sections.title: The Metric Container Object Format
sections.content:
Metrics and constraints travel inside the DAG Metric Container defined in RFC 6550, which is carried in DODAG Information Object (DIO) messages. Each Routing Metric/Constraint object starts with a common header: an 8-bit Routing-MC-Type, flag bits, a 3-bit A field, a 4-bit Prec field and an 8-bit Length for the object body, from 0 to 255 bytes.

The flags say how to read the object. C set means a constraint, cleared means a metric. O marks an optional constraint (cleared means mandatory). R set means the metric is recorded along the path, with each node adding a sub-object; cleared means it is aggregated, with each node updating one value. P is set when some node could not record the metric.

For aggregated metrics, A says how: 0 additive, 1 maximum, 2 minimum, 3 multiplicative. Prec (0 to 15, with 0 the highest precedence) ranks objects when several metrics are present, so that they act as tiebreakers. An object may also carry TLVs; unrecognized TLVs MUST be silently ignored but still propagated in DIOs. Because the container cannot exceed 255 bytes, multiple containers can be used and are treated as one long container.
sections.plainLanguage: Every measurement comes in an envelope with a label saying what it is, whether it is a rule or just a score, and how important it is compared to the others.

sections.title: Node Metrics and Constraints
sections.content:
Three objects describe nodes. The Node State and Attribute (NSA, type 1) object has two flags: A says the node can act as a traffic aggregator, and O says the node is overloaded and may not be able to process traffic. The RFC recommends avoiding frequent changes of the overload bit to prevent routing oscillations.

The Node Energy (NE, type 2) object reports how a node is powered. The T field gives the node type: 0 mains-powered, 1 battery-powered, 2 energy scavenger. The E bit says whether the 8-bit E_E field carries an estimated percentage of remaining energy. For a battery node, E_E is the current expected lifetime divided by the desired minimum lifetime, in percent; for a scavenger it is the power provided divided by the power consumed, in percent. As a constraint, the I bit says whether nodes of the given type must be included or excluded. The RFC notes that raw percentages are only comparable when nodes have similar energy storage.

The Hop Count (HP, type 3) object counts traversed nodes. As a metric, each visited node increments it, and the first node to insert it sets it to 1. As a constraint, the DAG root sets a maximum number of hops; once reached, no other node can join that path.
sections.plainLanguage: A node can say "I am plugged into the wall", "I run on a battery" or "I run on sunshine", how much energy it has left, and whether it is too busy. A rule can then say "only use plugged-in nodes" or "no more than this many hops".

sections.title: Link Metrics and Constraints
sections.content:
Five objects describe links. Throughput (type 4) is a 32-bit unsigned value in bytes per second, and the first sub-object MUST be the most recently estimated actual throughput. Latency (type 5) is a 32-bit unsigned value in microseconds and can be used as an additive path metric or as a limit such as a maximum latency.

Link reliability has two forms. The Link Quality Level (LQL, type 6) is a discrete value from 0 to 7, where 0 means unknown and 1 is the highest quality. It can only be recorded as a metric, and each sub-object pairs a value with a counter of how many links had that level, which compresses the message. The ETX object (type 7) carries the Expected Transmission Count, the number of transmissions a node expects to make to deliver a packet. ETX is encoded in 16 bits as ETX times 128, rounded to the nearest whole number; for example 3.569 becomes 457, and anything above 511.9921875 is sent as the maximum, 65535. The RFC mentions ETX = 1 / (Df * Dr) as one possible formula but does not mandate it.

The Link Color (LC, type 8) object is an administrative 10-bit link constraint, a set of flag bits whose meaning the implementer defines (the example given is a bit meaning an encrypted link). Used as a recorded metric it counts links per color; used as a constraint, a sub-object with an I bit says whether links of that color must be included or excluded.
sections.plainLanguage: For each road between two nodes you can note how fast it is, how long messages take, how often messages get lost, and a custom sticker such as "encrypted". Routes can then favour or avoid roads with certain stickers.

sections.title: Using Dynamic Metrics Carefully
sections.content:
The RFC warns that dynamic metrics are not trivial and may cause routing instabilities, and notes that dynamic metrics were already experimented with in ARPANET 2. Its guidance is to control the pace of change. Multi-threshold algorithms MAY be used to decide when to send updates, and low-pass filtering or hysteresis should be used when practical to avoid rapid fluctuations. Different metrics may use different reporting rates.

When the container holds one aggregated metric, the ordering is implied by its type: lower is better for Hop Count, Link Latency and ETX, while higher is better for Node Energy and Throughput. With several aggregated metrics, Prec orders them. The RFC's example is Hop Count as the primary criterion, LQL second and Node Energy as the final tiebreaker, using Prec values 0, 1 and 2. If several metrics have the same Prec value, behavior is implementation dependent.

In the presence of a constraint, a node MUST include a metric of the same type, which is used to check whether the constraint is met. A node MUST NOT change the content of the constraint. If more than one object of a type appears where only one is allowed, the second MUST be silently ignored.
sections.plainLanguage: If a team changed its plan every time the wind blew a little differently, nothing would get done. Nodes should only announce changes that really matter, and not too often.

sections.title: IANA Registries
sections.content: IANA created a top-level registry called "RPL Routing Metric/Constraint" with sub-registries for object types (0 to 255, with 0 unassigned), TLVs, the common header flag and A fields, the NSA flags, the Hop-Count flags and the node type field. New allocations follow the IETF Review policy of RFC 5226. The eight object types defined here are numbered 1 to 8, and no TLVs are registered yet.
sections.plainLanguage: There is an official list, kept by IANA, of the numbers that stand for each kind of measurement, so everybody uses the same codes.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A malicious node could falsely advertise good metrics so that it is chosen as preferred next-hop router and can intercept packets. An attacker could also make intermittent attacks on a link to keep changing its quality metric and cause fluctuation in the DODAG. The RFC RECOMMENDS that RPL implementations stop advertising metrics for highly unstable links that may be subject to attacks.

Metrics can also reveal weak spots, such as an unreliable link or a node low on energy. The RFC RECOMMENDS considering which metrics to use and how much they reveal, or using the security measures of RFC 6550. Since the metrics travel inside RPL messages, the RPL security mechanisms apply.
sections.plainLanguage: A cheater could shout "my road is great, come this way!" to steal your messages. Nodes should be careful whom they believe, and not give away which of their roads are weak.

fields.name: Routing-MC-Type
fields.desc: Identifies the kind of metric or constraint object; managed by IANA.

fields.name: Res Flags
fields.desc: Reserved bits; MUST be zero on transmission and ignored on receipt.

fields.name: P
fields.desc: Set when some node could not record a recorded metric.

fields.name: C
fields.desc: Set for a constraint, cleared for a metric.

fields.name: O
fields.desc: For constraints: set means optional, cleared means mandatory.

fields.name: R
fields.desc: For metrics: set means recorded, cleared means aggregated.

fields.name: A
fields.desc: How an aggregated metric combines: additive, maximum, minimum or multiplicative.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Length of the object body in bytes, 0 to 255.

items.label: Node Energy
items.desc: Power source type and estimated remaining energy.

items.label: Link Quality Level
items.desc: Discrete value 0 to 7, recorded with counters.

items.label: Link ETX
items.desc: Expected transmission count, encoded as ETX times 128.
